paras.en: The Collision Engineering program is active at partner schools across the country, including College of Lake County in Grayslake, Ill.; Contra Costa College in San Pablo, Calif.; Parkland College in Champaign, Ill.; Metropolitan Community College in Omaha, Neb.; Sandhills Community College in Pinehurst, N.C.; North Dakota State College of Science in Wahpeton, N.D.; and El Camino College in Torrance, Calif.

“Through Collision Engineering, I graduated with a degree, real experience and a clear path forward,” said Karina Badillo, Collision Engineering graduate from the College of Lake County. “This industry is moving fast, and Collision Engineering prepared me to move with it. Donations like the one made possible by the GEICO Philanthropic Foundation will help more people get that same start.”
Employers, educators and others interested in helping students explore collision repair careers can learn about the program and ways to get involved at beacollisionengineer.com.

articles.title: Ohio Mutual Insurance Group launches ‘Trusted Repair Program’ DRP with CrashBay
articles.author: Lurah Lowery

paras.en: CrashBay is now powering a direct repair program for Ohio Mutual Insurance Group.
According to CrashBay, Ohio Mutual announced the “Trusted Repair Program” earlier this year. CrashBay says Ohio Mutual was looking to streamline claims handling and improve shop relationships.
“Through its partnership with CrashBay, it now has one coordinated repair workflow that improves consistency, communication, and visibility across the entire process,” a CrashBay blog post states.
CrashBay says the workflow manages estimates, supplements, re-inspections, and communication between the carrier and its repair shops.

The post adds that the program “connects parties involved in automobile claims involving Ohio Mutual members with a trusted network of repair facilities and provides coordinated support throughout the repair process, from first notice of loss through completed repairs.”
CrashBay notes that it is the intelligence layer for collision coordination, and doesn’t own repair facilities nor perform repairs.

“Regional carriers like Ohio Mutual know their policyholders and their markets, and they want a repair program that reflects that without building the machinery to run one,” said John Harvey, founder and CEO of CrashBay, in the post. “We give them a coordinated, consistent repair process that fits how their claims team already works, so they get the benefits of a direct repair program without the administrative weight.”
The post adds that the program launch reflects a broader shift in how some regional carriers approach direct repair.
“Managing a shop network, keeping the workflow consistent, and coordinating communication no longer has to rest solely on internal resources,” the post states.

Clare Krumlauf, Ohio Mutual Insurance Group claims AVP, adds: “While insureds and claimants always retain the ultimate choice of which repair facility to use, the partnership with CrashBay adds another way for us to deliver on the trust our members place in Ohio Mutual. The program expands access to quality repair options while providing greater visibility and coordination throughout the repair process, helping those involved in a claim to navigate a challenging time with confidence.”
Featured image provided by Ohio Mutual Insurance Group

articles.title: CFA urges appointment of consumer-focused insurance commissioner in Texas
articles.author: Teresa Moss

paras.en: The Consumer Federation of America (CFA) urges Texas Governor-Elect Gina Hinojosa, in a letter sent to her this week, to appoint a new insurance commissioner who focuses on consumers.

“With escalating auto and homeowners insurance rates and harmful pricing practices that leave many consumers paying higher prices, the appointment of a pro-consumer Insurance Commissioner is essential to lowering the cost burden of insurance for millions of Texans,” states the letter signed by Douglas Heller, CFA director of insurance, and Michael DeLong, CFA research and advocacy associate.

According to the letter, the Texas Department of Insurance (TDI) is one of the best-resourced departments in the nation. However, over the last several years, the department has focused on protecting insurer interests and profits at the expense of consumers, the letter adds.
A consumer-focused leader at TDI could bring financial relief across the state, the letter states. Bob Hunter, a former TDI commissioner and CFA director of insurance, is pointed to as an example.
“Texas’s insurance market is one of the largest in the nation, worth about $294 billion and with more than $106 billion in direct written property and casualty premiums in 2025,” the letter states.
It adds that TDI is tasked with ensuring insurance rates are not excessive, inadequate, or unfairly discriminatory and that companies pay claims fairly and expeditiously.
TDI requires auto insurance, but the market is unaffordable for many Texans, the letter states. It adds that an estimated 14.5% of motorists in the state are uninsured.

“High prices disproportionately harm low-income consumers and communities of color because insurers include socioeconomic and personal characteristics of customers in their pricing models,” the letter states.

It adds that credit history pushes up auto insurance premiums for Texas drivers with perfect driving records. Texans with “poor” credit pay 126% more for basic coverage required by state law, it states.
CFA states that drivers with perfect driving records but “poor” or even “good” credit pay more for coverage than drivers with “excellent” credit who have been convicted of drunk driving.

“Legal and regulatory actions around the country are revealing insurers’ aggressive strategies to unfairly delay, low-ball, and deny claim payments to consumers,” CFA says. “Recently, the state of Oklahoma filed lawsuits against Allstate and State Farm for allegedly maintaining secret standards (reportedly also deployed in Texas, according to the State Farm lawsuit) where they attempted to close as many homeowners claims as possible without paying the customer anything and to reduce payments as much as possible, in spite of their massive advertising campaigns promising otherwise.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The letter also warns of increasing AI use by insurers in all aspects of the insurance product cycle with insufficient regulatory guidance or constraints.

“We expect that this will not only further disempower consumers when they buy insurance and file claims, but it will reinforce long-standing racial and ethnic biases that have harmed communities of color for decades,” the letter states.

The new commissioner must advocate for legislative reforms, including bans on socioeconomic factors insurers use to surcharge consumers higher premiums, and the creation of a low-cost auto insurance program for low-income drivers, the letter states.

“The commissioner must also provide guidance to insurers and consumers on how to reduce risk and hold insurers accountable for any mistreatment of consumers, including delays, denials, and minimizations of claims,” the letter adds.

articles.title: CIC committee tackles suggestions for AI use in claims handling
articles.author: Teresa Moss

paras.en: AI is involved in the auto claims handling process, but regulations have yet to catch up, Jill Tuggle, Auto Body Association of Texas executive director, said during the Collision Industry Conference’s most recent meeting held in Las Vegas.
The National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) approved a model bulletin in 2023 on insurer AI use that 25 states and Washington, D.C., have adopted, she said.
None of the states that have adopted the model require a human to make the final call on claim denials, she added.
An NAIC survey also found 88% of auto insurers are using or exploring AI, she said.
“We still have a long way to go,” Tuggle said.
AI now touches vehicle intake, photo review, estimating, valuation, and claim closure, she added.
Currently, a vehicle is often inspected by a shop and a field adjuster who agree on the required repairs, Tuggle explained. The estimate then goes to a central review team.

“We’re not really sure who is behind that right now,” Tuggle said. “AI is scrubbing the files in many cases, and these algorithms are built by the companies who are reviewing them. We’re not totally sure what the parameters are that are being set and how they’re writing the algorithms to take a look at these files.”
There are examples of automatic overrides for estimates that include more than eight hours of repair, Tuggle said.
A shop will reach out to a field adjuster to discuss the changes to the estimate, she adds. The shop is told the adjuster is no longer on the claim and the shop must call customer service.

“That’s when we start hitting brick walls,” Tuggle said. “So who actually made the final decision? So the issue here is the attribution gap. Who observed the car, the field adjuster? Who modified the estimate? The central team and their AI scrubbers? Who knows? That’s often very unclear. But the field adjuster is still named at the bottom.”
The CIC Governmental Committee found an example of an AI-handled claim where the shop estimate was about $2,500, Tuggle said. It came back from the central review team at $438.
The claim was closed because it was lower than the deductible, Tuggle said. She added there was no recourse for the customer on the claim decision.
“What consumers should be able to count on is knowing when AI material has shaped their claim and know who made the decision and how to reach out to them,” Tuggle said.
When asked, 67% of the CIC audience also believed consumers should know when AI is used in the claim handling process.

NAIC’s AI model is built on the existing Unfair Claims Settlement Practices Act, she explains. It covers claims and fraud detection; states controls should scale with potential harm to consumers; and states that decisions cannot be inaccurate, arbitrary, or unfairly discriminatory.
It also requires insurance companies to set clear decision authority and escalation paths, test data and models, monitor for drifts, keep records, notify consumers of AI use, and oversee vendors.

Tuggle said the bulletin doesn’t require claim-level notice that AI shaped the estimate. It also doesn’t require a change log or final author on the estimate, a named accountable reviewer, or duties for shops or vendors.
There should be more oversight depending on the consequence, Tuggle said.
For example, disclosure isn’t necessary for administrative work such as scheduling, transcription, and document searching.
Perhaps there should be AI disclosure for AI drafts with review by a qualified person and the ability to change the draft, she said.
In a third scenario, insurance companies should provide a disclosure with a named approver and a reason when AI removes repairs, totals a vehicle, or flags fraud, Tuggle said.
A meaningful human review needs to meet five criteria, she said.
- “Competence: Can spot the technical error;
- “Evidence: Sees the photos, not just AI summary;
- “Time: Not racing a productivity quota;
- “Authority: Can override without layers of approval; and
- “Permission: Can disagree without penalty.”
Tuggle asked, “At the end of the day, when you’ve got an estimate where so many different entities and people have influenced it, who owns it?”

”That’s kind of one of the major issues,” she continued. “You have your data provider who supplies the inputs and your AI vendor; they’re building the models, the algorithms for the scrubbing software that they’re using at the central review areas. And then we’ve got our estimating platform, which embeds it into the workflow. Insurers approve or deny the claim, and the repair facilities perform the repair.”
Tuggle asked whether there could be shared responsibility that is also symmetrical in the process.
The committee also suggests duties for consequential AI. This includes AI disclosing material and preserving every estimate version.

It should also attribute credit to who inspected the estimate, which system was used, changes made, and who made the changes, Tuggle said. She added that insurance companies should explain the basis for each change and provide an escalation option to a human who can reverse it.
The name also must mean something, she said.
“The field adjuster’s name at the bottom of the file is not enough, and it’s not really getting us anywhere right now,” she said. “So, proposed again, a human decides the safety and critical items.”

The committee also proposes that a qualified human must approve any cuts to procedures such as structural repairs, airbags, seatbelts, restraints, scans, ADAS calibration, fraud flags, and other safety-critical items.
“AI can advise it, but it can’t be the only reason for denial,” Tuggle said.
James Spears, Tractable head of automotive AI, said during a panel discussion that it would be difficult to imagine all the ways that AI touches insurance claims.

“AI begins at policy acquisition,” Spears said. “AI begins before they even have a customer, right? AI is used in the way that you market. AI is used once you close a policy. AI is used in underwriting. AI is used all throughout in a number of ways.”
Many assume AI has evil intent, but it can increase claim speed and accuracy, Spears said.
He explained that the AI models the general public uses aren’t as advanced as the models insurance companies use. However, he said AI will advance significantly in the coming years.
Jerry McNee of Ultimate Collision agreed that AI benefits the user.
Before AI, a shop manually went through everything and took time pulling the repair processes. It took additional time to verify, he added.
Humans also have errors and miss procedures, he said.

“We have to get ahead of it, and we have to understand it, and we have to put it to work,” McNee said. “There still has to be some human interaction and touch on it, in order to proof it and make sure.”

“The best way to employ AI is to only use it as a tool that takes some mundane task off of your team,” Spears said. “Then push that team towards the customer. That’s where you really make a difference.”
He added that he disagrees with “straight-through” processing where a human never touches a claim.
The insurance and repair industries should work together to create rules AI can work within, he said.

“Ninety-five percent of AI will get you to yes with shared rules very quickly,” Spears said. “The other 5%, that’s going to be your escalation, and that’s when you get humans talking about it. That’s the way I would play the game. If I was sitting in a carrier’s chair right now, I would have shared rules with every one of my DRPs.”
AI can help speed up parts and rental car deliveries, Spears added.
When Tuggle asked whether consumers should be notified of AI use, Spears said they should.
“But here’s the deal: It’s not going to shock a consumer,” Spears said. “Because everything in their life has AI.”
“Absolutely, consumers should be informed, especially on the decision-making when it comes to their vehicle or their policy or returning the car back to its previous condition,” McNee said.
Jill Tuggle, Auto Body Association of Texas executive director, James Spears, Tractable head of automotive AI, Jerry McNee of Ultimate Collision during CIC in Las Vegas.

articles.title: Brake Job: 2020–2026 Buick Encore GX
articles.author: Andrew Markel

paras.en: I was recently working on an ASE A5 test-prep article, and we reached the section on parking brakes. Most parking brakes act on the rear wheels, so the test is structured around that arrangement. But some vehicles have parking brakes on the front wheels. I knew that some older Saabs and Datsuns used front-wheel parking brakes. One modern example is the Buick Encore GX.

On these models, pulling the park-brake switch sends a signal to the Electronic Brake Control Module. The module supplies 12 volts to the apply-control circuits and ground to the release-control circuits, activating the left and right park-brake actuators and applying the brakes.

Pressing the switch sends a signal to the module to release the brakes. The module supplies 12 volts to the release-control circuits and ground to the apply-control circuits, activating the actuators and releasing the brakes. Depending on the vehicle, the switch may be a push-button style. Pressing it commands the parking brakes to apply or release based on their current position.

The parking brake will release automatically if the engine is running, the vehicle is shifted into gear, and the driver attempts to move off. Avoid rapid acceleration while the parking brake is applied to help preserve the parking-brake lining.
The Electronic Brake Control Module, also called the Brake System Control Module, controls the park-brake motor circuits and runs diagnostics to verify that they are operating properly.

To replace the brake pads, the park-brake caliper pistons must be fully retracted. There are two ways to put the parking brake into service mode. The preferred method is to use a scan tool with a service-mode function. If you do not have a compatible scan tool, use this procedure:
- Turn the ignition on with the engine off.
- Press the accelerator pedal halfway down.
- Move the park-brake switch to the release position and hold it for 10 seconds. Release the switch.
- Within five seconds, move the switch to the release position again.

The actuator bolts to the back of the caliper and is not included with a replacement caliper. If you remove the actuator, GM recommends replacing the caliper’s O-ring. Front-wheel parking brakes may be a novelty, but they make an interesting piece of trivia to test your technician friends on.

articles.title: What Tire Wear Reveals About Suspension and Alignments
articles.author: Doug Kaufman

paras.en: A driver rolls into the shop complaining that their tires are wearing out faster than expected. The vehicle drives reasonably well, and there are no obvious suspension noises. But a closer look at the tread tells a different story.

Uneven tire wear can reveal problems with alignment, suspension components, tire inflation and ride control. Learning how to recognize these patterns gives technicians a valuable diagnostic advantage.
The key is understanding what each wear pattern means and knowing which components to inspect next.
Start With Tire Pressure and Tread Depth
Before recommending an alignment or replacing suspension components, check the basics.
Inspect all four tires. Measure and record tread depth across the inner, center and outer portions of each tire. Compare the readings to identify differences in wear.

Next, check inflation pressure against the vehicle manufacturer’s specifications. Underinflation often increases wear along both shoulders, while sustained overinflation can increase center tread wear.
Don’t overlook the tire pressure monitoring system (TPMS). A warning light, damaged sensor or incorrect pressure setting may contribute to a problem that has gone unnoticed.
Also look for mismatched tires, damaged wheels and evidence of missed tire rotations.
These initial checks help determine whether the cause is tire maintenance, vehicle geometry or a mechanical problem.
Inner-Edge Wear: Check Camber, Toe and Ride Height
When the inside shoulder wears faster than the rest of the tread, alignment geometry should be one of the first areas to investigate.
Negative camber means the top of the wheel tilts inward relative to the vehicle. Excessive negative camber can place additional load on the inner shoulder.
Toe settings also matter. When wheels point too far inward or outward relative to the vehicle’s direction of travel, the tires scrub against the road instead of rolling cleanly.
- Problems with an air suspension system
Independent rear suspensions deserve particular attention. Worn bushings can change wheel geometry during acceleration, braking and cornering.
Shop tip: Measure ride height before performing an alignment. If the suspension is sitting below specification, adjusting alignment angles alone may not solve the problem.
Outer-Edge Wear: Inspect Alignment and Body Control
Excessive wear on the outside shoulder may indicate an alignment problem or excessive loading during cornering.
Positive camber, incorrect toe settings and worn suspension components can contribute to outer-edge wear.
Consider how the vehicle is driven. Crossovers and SUVs have relatively high centers of gravity, which can increase weight transfer during turns.
When springs, shocks or struts no longer control suspension movement effectively, the tire may experience additional loading and irregular wear.
Diagnostic reminder: Outer-edge wear does not automatically mean the shocks are bad. Verify alignment and mechanical condition before recommending replacement parts.
Feathering occurs when the tread blocks develop a sharp edge on one side and a smoother, rounded edge on the other.
You may not notice feathering immediately during a visual inspection. Carefully running your hand across the tread in opposite directions can help identify the pattern.
Feathering commonly indicates an incorrect toe setting.
However, toe can change when worn steering or suspension components move under load. That means the alignment readings may not tell the entire story.
Check for looseness in tie rods, control arm bushings and other steering components before making adjustments.
Remember that changing camber or caster can affect toe. That’s why toe is normally adjusted after other applicable alignment angles.
Cupping and Scalloping: Look Beyond Alignment
Cupping creates irregular high and low spots around the tire’s circumference. The pattern may resemble a series of shallow dips in the tread.
- Loose or damaged suspension components
Shocks and struts help control wheel movement as the vehicle travels over bumps. If they lose damping ability, the tire may move excessively and develop irregular wear.
However, wheel imbalance can create similar symptoms.
Shop example: A driver complains of a humming noise that increases with road speed. The rear tires show scalloped wear, but there is no obvious wheel-bearing play.
Before replacing a bearing, inspect the tire surfaces, check wheel balance and evaluate suspension condition. Tire noise can sometimes resemble a failing wheel bearing.
A vehicle’s suspension geometry is designed around a specified operating height.
When springs weaken or suspension components wear, ride height can change. That affects camber, toe and the position of suspension control arms.
A small height difference may have a meaningful impact on tire wear.
Measure ride height using the manufacturer’s procedure and compare the results against specification. Don’t assume that springs are healthy simply because the vehicle appears level.
On vehicles with electronic air suspension, check for leaks and verify that ride-height sensors and calibration are operating correctly.
Don’t Forget Rear Alignment and Thrust Angle
Tire wear problems aren’t always limited to the front axle.

The thrust angle describes the direction the rear wheels point relative to the vehicle’s centerline. If the rear wheels are not aligned correctly, the driver may need to compensate with the steering wheel to keep the vehicle moving straight.
That condition can contribute to unusual tire wear and a steering wheel that appears off-center.
A four-wheel alignment can help identify these problems, particularly on vehicles with independent rear suspension.
When uneven tire wear enters the shop, use a consistent inspection process.
- Verify the complaint. Ask when the wear started and whether the vehicle pulls, vibrates or makes noise.
- Inspect the tires. Record tread depths, tire sizes, inflation pressures and visible wear patterns.
- Check the suspension. Inspect steering components, bushings, springs, shocks and struts.
- Measure ride height. Compare measurements with factory specifications.
- Check alignment. Review camber, caster, toe and thrust angle where applicable.
- Verify the repair. Correct the cause, evaluate tire safety and explain the findings to the customer.
The Takeaway: Let the Tires Guide Your Diagnosis
Tires are more than replaceable wear items. They provide clues about how the vehicle’s steering, suspension and alignment systems are working together.
Recognizing those clues helps technicians diagnose problems earlier, protect customers’ tire investments and avoid unnecessary repairs.
The next time a vehicle comes into the bay, take a closer look at its tires. What is the tread trying to tell you?

articles.title: Think Twice Before Erasing Trouble Codes
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: Counter pros should avoid erasing diagnostic trouble codes when customers request it. Clearing codes without fixing the underlying problem will only temporarily turn off the check engine light.

Erasing codes also deletes valuable freeze-frame data that technicians need for accurate diagnosis. Additionally, clearing codes resets emissions readiness monitors, potentially affecting vehicle emissions testing.

articles.title: Replacing an Oil Filter Housing With an Integrated Oil Cooler
articles.author: Andrew Markel

paras.en: A leak at the oil filter housing isn’t limited to a gasket for its explanation. On many late-model import engines, the housing is part of a larger module that manages oil filtration and temperature, and may also contain sensors, thermostats and coolant passages.

Look at many late-model European engines and you’ll find an assembly bolted to the side of the block or mounted in the engine’s V. It may hold the oil filter and oil cooler, along with thermostats, valves or sensors. That arrangement helps fit more functions into a crowded engine compartment, but it can turn a straightforward oil leak into a more involved repair.

The design reflects two pressures on engine development: packaging and temperature control. Modern engines often use oil to operate variable valve timing systems and, in some engines, cylinder deactivation hardware. The oil must reach these components at the required pressure and volume, while staying within the engine’s operating temperature range.

Oil cooling has changed to meet those needs. Some older imports used an air-to-oil cooler mounted near the radiator, with oil routed through an adapter between the filter and its mounting base. Many later designs moved to a liquid-to-liquid cooler, often sandwiched between the engine and oil filter. Coolant warms the oil more quickly after a cold start and carries away heat once the oil is hot. Integrating the filter, cooler and related controls into a single module saves space and can simplify assembly.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: A liquid-to-liquid cooler transfers heat between engine oil and coolant through plates or passages inside a compact heat exchanger. The fluids remain separate; heat moves through the metal between them. Because coolant can carry heat away efficiently in a relatively small space, the cooler can be packaged close to the engine without the airflow requirements of a front-mounted cooler.

Many designs use stacked plates to create a large heat-transfer area. That compact construction has a service tradeoff: narrow internal passages can retain debris. If a major engine failure sends metal fragments through the lubrication system, an oil change may not remove everything lodged in the cooler. Manufacturer guidance for some engine repairs calls for replacing the cooler and related components when bearing debris contaminates the oil circuit, because cleaning cannot reliably remove all of it.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Oil around the housing does not automatically mean that the housing itself has failed. The leak may come from the housing-to-engine seal, the cooler seals, the filter cap or another component above the assembly. Oil can travel down the engine and collect at the lowest point, making the source hard to identify.

Clean the area and inspect it closely. If necessary, use an approved leak-detection dye and re-check the engine after running it. Look for coolant residue as well as oil. A leak between the oil and coolant passages can cause contamination in either direction, depending on operating pressures and the failure. If the coolant is oily or the oil appears milky, diagnose the source before deciding what to replace.

Check the vehicle-specific service information before starting. The procedure may require draining coolant, removing intake or accessory components, or following a particular sequence to release the housing. Some assemblies include separate cooler seals; others are serviced as a unit. Check whether the manufacturer specifies replacement bolts, sealants, tightening sequences or a special coolant bleeding procedure.

Start with a cool engine. Drain the coolant if the service procedure calls for it, then disconnect electrical connectors and coolant hoses without stressing aged plastic fittings. Clean debris from around the assembly before opening the oil and coolant passages. Dirt that falls into an exposed passage can circulate through the engine.

Clean the engine’s sealing surface carefully. Avoid abrasive discs and aggressive scraping that can gouge or distort the surface. Keep debris out of the oil and coolant passages. If baked-on gasket material is difficult to remove, use a compatible gasket remover and a suitable non-damaging tool. Follow product directions and keep solvent out of the engine.

Install new seals in the correct locations and orientation. Lubricate them only if the service information calls for it. Tighten fasteners in the specified sequence and to the specified torque, using a torque wrench. Remember that uneven or excessive clamping force can distort a housing, damage a cooler or cause a new leak. Avoid adding sealant unless the procedure specifies it; excess sealant can squeeze into passages.
Address Contamination and Verify the Repair

If oil has entered the cooling system, replacing the failed cooler or housing may not be enough. Oil can remain in the radiator, heater core, hoses and expansion tank. Follow the vehicle manufacturer’s cleaning procedure and use only products approved for that cooling system. A 2025 service bulletin, for example, warns against using unvalidated detergents because they may damage seals or metal components. Replace contaminated parts when the prescribed procedure calls for it.

If coolant has entered the oil, change the oil and filter after the leak is repaired, and follow the manufacturer’s guidance on whether further oil changes or inspections are needed. If the engine has suffered a mechanical failure that released metal debris, do not assume flushing will make the cooler reusable. The passages can retain contamination that may return to the engine after startup.

Refill the fluids to the correct levels, and bleed the cooling system according to the application; some vehicles require a particular sequence or electronic procedure. Start the engine and check for leaks as it warms up. Confirm that the oil and coolant levels remain stable, then re-check the housing and surrounding area after a road test and cooldown.

articles.title: NMG Gives UAC, Precision Vendor of the Year Awards
articles.author: Alex Crissey

paras.en: NexaMotion Group (NMG) named UAC (Universal Air Conditioner, Inc.) and Precision International the recipients of its first annual Vendor of the Year award.

According to NMG, honorees were selected by NMG’s executive and supply chain leadership on “availability, quality and responsiveness, and on a harder test: how far the supplier was willing to go in service of NMG’s strategy and its customers’ success.”

“Anyone can fill an order. Our best partners help us build the business,” said Scott Weinstein, president of NexaMotion Group. “UAC and Precision International show up in the planning room, not just on the loading dock. They bring us coverage before our customers ask for it, they invest in our people and our shops, and when we make bold moves as a company they are right beside us. That is partnership, and it is what this award was created to honor.”

articles.title: Static vs. Dynamic ADAS Calibrations
articles.author: Christian Hinton

paras.en: Choosing between static and dynamic ADAS calibration depends on the procedure specified by the vehicle manufacturer. Regardless of the method, the vehicle and its surroundings must meet the manufacturer’s requirements.
ADAS systems affected by a repair may need to be calibrated, relearned or re-zeroed. Terminology may vary, but the purpose is to establish an accurate reference point for the system.
A static calibration is performed while the vehicle remains stationary. Technicians position targets at exact distances and heights, and the targets must also be square to the vehicle’s centerline.
The vehicle must meet specified requirements for weight, ride height, tire pressure, fluid levels, lighting and background conditions.
Dynamic calibration takes place while driving. The technician places the system into calibration mode and drives the vehicle under specified conditions.
During the drive, the sensors verify that they can identify the roadway, recognize objects and align correctly with the vehicle’s centerline.
Extra weight, improper tire pressure, incorrect ride height or environmental interference can cause calibration to fail. These conditions can also establish an inaccurate reference.

Whether the procedure is static or dynamic, technicians must follow the manufacturer’s instructions exactly. ADAS calibration depends on precision, and even small inconsistencies can affect system performance.

articles.title: NTN Volunteer Event Supports Local Food Pantry
articles.author: Alex Crissey

paras.en: NTN Bearing Corp. of America held its Community Spirit & Engagement Event at the Elk Grove Township Food Pantry in Elk Grove Village, Illinois, on Tuesday, October 27. A team of twelve NTN employees volunteered to help combat food insecurity and support local families ahead of Thanksgiving.

Volunteers spent the morning assembling approximately 400 Thanksgiving food bags that will be distributed to families throughout the community. Designed as a “trick-or-treat” style shopping experience, team members worked together at various food stations, collecting and packing items including cooking oil, canned vegetables, canned pumpkin, mashed potatoes, macaroni and cheese, gravy, brownie mix, and other household necessities.

In the afternoon, NTN employees assisted pantry staff with organizing and storing five pallets of donated food. According to the food pantry manager, the work completed by the NTN team in a few hours would have taken the pantry’s regular staff and volunteers up to a month to accomplish.

NTN’s Community Spirit & Engagement Program, launched in January 2023, includes contributing time and resources to charitable organizations, encouraging employees to take an active role in the local community, and building partnerships with other groups and organizations.

The Elk Grove Township Food Pantry provides food assistance and related support services to residents facing food insecurity, serving approximately 1,100 families each month through a client-choice model that allows households to access nutritious food and household essentials in a dignified and convenient manner. Through partnerships with community organizations, donors, and volunteers, the pantry helps ensure local families have access to the resources they need throughout the year and is expected to distribute the Thanksgiving food bags assembled during the event to nearly 900 families this holiday season.

articles.title: AACF Golf Tournament Raises Record $700,000
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: The Automotive Aftermarket Charitable Foundation (AACF) celebrated the success of its 34th annual Bob Schoeberl Memorial Charity Golf Tournament. The event took place Nov. 1-2 at Spanish Trail Country Club in Las Vegas. The sold-out event brought together 216 golfers and other automotive aftermarket industry supporters for two days of networking and competition.

Fundraising activities included the tournament, live auction, prize drawings and golf pro experiences. These activities raised nearly $700,000, marking the highest total in the event’s history. The funds will help AACF provide financial assistance to aftermarket families facing unexpected hardships.
AACF Tournament Supports Aftermarket Families

“When a member of the automotive aftermarket community faces an unexpected hardship, the support of this industry can make all the difference,” said John Kairys, executive director of AACF. “The generosity of everyone who participated in this year’s tournament will help ensure that individuals and families facing some of life’s most difficult moments know they aren’t alone. We’re thankful and appreciative that this community comes together year after year for such an important cause.”
Historic Hole-in-One Highlights Tournament

Among this year’s tournament highlights, Sean McLoraine became the first participant in the event’s 34-year history to win the hole-in-one contest. Interstate Batteries sponsored the contest, which featured a new 2026 Toyota Tundra as its grand prize.

“I look forward to this tournament every year because I love seeing our industry come together to give back to the people who make it what it is,” said Jeff Helfrich, AACF golf committee chairman. “To raise a record amount for aftermarket families and have Sean McLoraine make the first hole-in-one for a vehicle in our 34 years of playing this event made this a year I’ll always remember. Congratulations to Sean on his new Toyota Tundra and thank you to Interstate Batteries for sponsoring the contest.”

articles.title: Gates to Acquire Nitta’s Stakes in Five Asian Markets
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: Gates Industrial Corporation Ltd. announced an agreement to acquire Nitta Corporation’s interests in five Asia-Pacific joint ventures. The transaction will give Gates full ownership of its power transmission businesses in China, India, Thailand, Korea and Singapore. Gates also will sell its interest in the Japan joint venture to Nitta.

The joint venture helped broaden Gates’ reach into emerging economies in the Asia-Pacific region. Since 1986, Gates has held a 51% ownership stake in each joint venture entity. Gates has consolidated the entities’ financial results into its own reporting.
The transaction will allow Gates to operate in Asia-Pacific through a wholly owned platform. It also reinforces the company’s long-term commitment to the region.
Gates anticipates several benefits from the transaction, including:

- Increasing reported earnings per share by eliminating the noncontrolling interest associated with the joint venture. Gates estimates the transaction will increase annual adjusted earnings per share (EPS) by $0.02 on a pro forma basis.
- Expanding Gates’ strategic flexibility to independently pursue growth initiatives in the Asia-Pacific region.
- Providing Gates with greater access to foreign cash reserves.
- Mitigating future restructuring investments.
- Simplifying Gates’ financial reporting.
Gates will pay Nitta approximately $40.2 million in dividends and a net $112 million for equity interests. The equity payment remains subject to certain post-closing adjustments.
Gates has historically consolidated the joint venture for accounting purposes. As a result, a portion of the joint venture’s revenue and profitability will transfer to Nitta.

Gates estimates the transaction will reduce its annualized 2027 consolidated sales by approximately $88 million to $108 million. The company also expects a reduction of approximately $26 million to $32 million in annualized 2027 adjusted EBITDA.

“We have built a profitable, growing business under Gates’ leadership across Asia-Pacific through a longstanding, collaborative relationship with Nitta. Taking full ownership in these markets gives Gates greater flexibility to pursue our growth strategy in the region,” said Ivo Jurek, Chief Executive Officer of Gates Industrial Corporation. “In conjunction with Nitta, we will work closely with employees, customers, suppliers and relevant regulatory bodies to ensure continuity.”

The transaction will conclude the longstanding partnership. Gates expects to close the transaction in the first quarter of 2027. The closing remains subject to customary conditions, including required regulatory approvals.

articles.title: VIVE Collision Appoints Charlie Drake Chief Operating Officer
articles.author: Jason Stahl

paras.en: VIVE Collision announced that it appointed Charlie Drake chief operating officer (COO) earlier this year. Drake brings nearly 40 years of industry experience and a people-first leadership approach that supports VIVE’s commitment to its teammates, customers and communities.

With two decades in operations leadership at national collision repair organizations, Drake combines experience managing multi-location businesses with a practical understanding of the work happening in each repair facility. He is known for building strong teams, linking culture to performance and creating systems that support accountability and a consistent customer experience.

“Growing VIVE means making sure our people have the leadership and support to do their best work,” said Vartan Jerian, Jr., CEO and founder of VIVE Collision. “Charlie understands what it takes to run a successful collision repair organization and how much of that success comes down to the people in each location. His experience and approach will help us strengthen our operations while keeping our teammates and customers at the center of every decision.”

As COO, Drake will lead VIVE’s operations, working with its leadership teams to support performance across the organization. His appointment reinforces VIVE’s focus on “People, Process and Passion,” pairing investment in its people with the operational discipline needed to deliver high-quality repairs and earn customer trust.

articles.title: The 45-Day Rule: How Parts Stores Stop Financing Their Customers
articles.author: Bob Morgan

paras.en: Every parts store has an account like this. The shop buys a lot. The owner is a good guy. He pays — eventually. Meanwhile he’s 50 to 90 days out and asking for another special order “by Thursday.”

Here’s the hard truth I learned after about 15 years running stores on Long Island: volume you don’t collect isn’t volume. It’s a loan you never approved. Most stores aren’t short on sales. They’re short on cash because they’re quietly running a bank for their customers, with the special-order desk as the loan window.
The fix isn’t a collections agency or a nasty letter. It’s one rule, written down and used every single time.
If an account is 45 or more days past due and they want a special order, the special waits until the money is in the building.
That’s it. Shelf stock can still go out for cash. The relationship stays intact. But you stop ordering non-returnable, hard-to-restock parts for an account that hasn’t paid for the last batch.

Why special orders? A stocked part sold on account is a receivable. A special order for a slow-paying account is a receivable plus freight, a restocking fee and a part you may end up owning if the job falls through. That’s where slow accounts do the most damage, so that’s where the line goes.

Before the rule works, everyone at the counter has to agree on what “45 days” means. I count days past the due date, not days since the invoice. A Net 30 invoice dated June 12 is due July 12. On September 2, it’s 52 days past due — over the line.

If you’d rather age from the invoice date, fine. Pick one method, write it on the rule and never switch mid-argument. If your company already has a hold policy, use its number. The discipline matters more than the exact day.
The 45-day rule works because nobody gets surprised by it. The steps before it do the heavy lifting:
- Day 30 — a reminder, not a threat. “Invoice 1844 is at 30. Card or check on the next stop?”
- Day 35–40 — a human call. Not another statement they’re already ignoring. A person, by name, on the phone.
- Day 45 — credit hold for new specials. Shelf can still be cash. Specials wait.
- Day 60 — hard hold. No “just this once” unless a manager puts the amount and the date in writing.
Most accounts never reach day 45 once the day-30 and day-35 touches actually happen. The rule is the backstop, not the first move.
Give your counter people the exact words. Nobody should improvise a credit conversation with a regular at the register. At day 45:
“I can keep selling you what’s here if we’re cash. I can’t put another special in motion until 1844 is clear. I need you current so I can keep saying yes.”
“I like working with you. I can’t keep shipping on a 60-day balance. Let’s pick an amount for this week and a date for the rest. Until that starts, we’re cash.”
Those lines don’t threaten and don’t apologize. They state the rule and offer a path back. “I need you current so I can keep saying yes” puts you and the customer on the same side.

The most common way the rule breaks: “I’m not paying until you fix that core credit.” Freeze the one disputed line and research it. The rest of the balance is still due. Don’t let a $40 question hold up a $4,000 balance.
And if yelling breaks the rule, you’ve just taught every shop in town that yelling works. The rule has to hold for your biggest account, too.
A rule nobody checks turns into a suggestion. Once a week — I do it in a short Monday meeting — pull your aging and look at three things:
- Total dollars 45+ and 60+ days past due.
- A name and a next-call date next to every one of those accounts.
- Any special order that went out to a 45+ account, and who approved it.

A simple example (invented numbers): a store has $6,940 at 45+ days past due across two accounts. A fleet account on that list calls for a special. The counter person checks the list and uses the day-45 line. The special gets placed the afternoon the check clears. No fight, no exception, and the store isn’t fronting more parts to a customer who already owes $4,200.
- Export or write down your current aging.
- Highlight everything 45+ and 60+ days past due.
- Put a name and a next-call date on every one.
- Write the special-order rule on a sticky note at the counter where everyone can see it.
You can like the shop. You can need the volume. You still collect. The 45-day rule is how a parts store stops financing its customers and gets back to selling them parts.

articles.title: AACF Golf Tournament Raises Record $700,000
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: The Automotive Aftermarket Charitable Foundation (AACF) celebrated the success of its 34th annual Bob Schoeberl Memorial Charity Golf Tournament. The event took place Nov. 1-2 at Spanish Trail Country Club in Las Vegas. The sold-out event brought together 216 golfers and other automotive aftermarket industry supporters for two days of networking and competition.

Fundraising activities included the tournament, live auction, prize drawings and golf pro experiences. These activities raised nearly $700,000, marking the highest total in the event’s history. The funds will help AACF provide financial assistance to aftermarket families facing unexpected hardships.
AACF Tournament Supports Aftermarket Families

“When a member of the automotive aftermarket community faces an unexpected hardship, the support of this industry can make all the difference,” said John Kairys, executive director of AACF. “The generosity of everyone who participated in this year’s tournament will help ensure that individuals and families facing some of life’s most difficult moments know they aren’t alone. We’re thankful and appreciative that this community comes together year after year for such an important cause.”
Historic Hole-in-One Highlights Tournament

Among this year’s tournament highlights, Sean McLoraine became the first participant in the event’s 34-year history to win the hole-in-one contest. Interstate Batteries sponsored the contest, which featured a new 2026 Toyota Tundra as its grand prize.

“I look forward to this tournament every year because I love seeing our industry come together to give back to the people who make it what it is,” said Jeff Helfrich, AACF golf committee chairman. “To raise a record amount for aftermarket families and have Sean McLoraine make the first hole-in-one for a vehicle in our 34 years of playing this event made this a year I’ll always remember. Congratulations to Sean on his new Toyota Tundra and thank you to Interstate Batteries for sponsoring the contest.”

articles.title: The immune system 'remembers' germs by tweaking its epigenetics, study shows
articles.author: Nicoletta Lanese

paras.en: The immune system has several ways of remembering threats it's encountered and then mounting stronger defenses in the future. Now, a new study unpacks how cells keep one type of immune memory from fading, and the findings might matter for treating diseases like cancer and Alzheimer's disease.

The research zoomed in on immune cells' epigenetics — the methods that cells use to control genes without changing their underlying DNA codes. This can involve changing how DNA is packaged inside cells, for example. DNA molecules are typically wound around tiny spools inside cells, and their gene activity depends on how tightly or loosely they're wound. Molecules called epigenetic markers can grab hold of the spool to tweak how the DNA is wound and thus activate or silence certain genes.

Past research found epigenetic changes can prime immune cells against threats. The immune system's first line of defense — innate immune cells — can be switched into an activated state so they're ready to go if they encounter a germ. This form of immune memory, known as "trained immunity," broadly enhances the cells' defenses, enabling them to respond to threats more quickly and powerfully than "untrained" cells would.

To flip that switch in the cells, a molecule latches onto the spool that DNA is wound around, specifically near genes involved in sparking inflammation. That subtle molecular tweak "holds those genes poised for rapid activation," said Musa Mhlanga, a cell biologist and molecular geneticist at the Radboud Institute for Molecular Life Sciences in the Netherlands who wasn't involved in the new study.
However, scientists didn't know how that change was maintained over time.

The immune memory should have been destroyed soon after it was made, given that "the cell has enzymes whose entire job is to strip that mark off," Mhlanga told Live Science in an email. But somehow, the memory stuck. "So the obvious question was never really answered: how does a mark survive weeks or months against machinery actively removing it?" Mhlanga said.
The new study, published Oct. 30 in the journal Science Immunology, may answer that question.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The research investigated the phenomenon in mouse immune cells and live lab mice, as well as some human cells in lab dishes. Past studies hinted that, when immune cells switch into their "primed" state, their metabolism changes. This, in turn, drives up the production of a molecule called nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), which has long been known to help regulate how DNA gets packaged in cells.

In this case, though, the molecule took on a surprising role, Mhlanga said. NAD+ usually gets used up when enzymes orchestrate chemical reactions. But when it comes to the enzymes that normally erase immune cells' memory, called KDM5a, that wasn't the case.

NAD+ latches onto that epigenetic eraser but doesn't get used up in the process; instead, it shuts down KDM5a, as if it were pushing an "off" button. By restraining its memory eraser, the immune cell remains in a primed and activated state, ready to ignite inflammation when triggered.

In experiments with mice, the researchers found that reducing or eliminating NAD+ from immune cells prevented them from entering this primed state. In mice with cancer, this hobbled the immune system's ability to attack tumor cells.

Additionally, in aging mice, the team observed that NAD+ levels dwindle in concert with the innate immune system's ability to respond to threats. The research builds a convincing "molecular bridge" between those two facts, Mhlanga said, raising a hypothesis for why immunity gets worse with age.

Broadly, the research adds to scientists' understanding of how innate immune cells enter this primed, inflammatory state. This line of research may help scientists understand "why some vaccines protect against diseases they were never designed for," Mhlanga said.

For example, a tuberculosis vaccine called Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BDG) is thought to mount a broad immune response that may help stave off many conditions, from viral infections to Alzheimer's disease. (Some scientists think that Alzheimer's stems from a dysregulated immune response that BCG may help to normalize.)

While this line of research could have wide-ranging applications, the new study has some limitations. The researchers did a few experiments with human cells and backed up some of their findings in mice with data from human cancer patients. However, "the human data are thin by comparison with the mouse work," Mhlanga noted, so they bear further confirmation.

In the future, he'd be interested in studies exploring NAD+ in the context of the aging immune system, cancer and Alzheimer's disease. The recent research hints that pushing NAD+ to optimal levels could help counter each of these conditions.
But especially in cancer, where the disease's biology varies by the tumour type and stage, "it is not a simple 'more NAD+ is better' story," he cautioned, "and I'd resist it being written as one."

articles.title: New study rewrites the role of a major speech hub in the brain
articles.author: RJ Mackenzie

paras.en: A new study has rewritten the role of one of the brain's major speech hubs, opening new possibilities for treating people who can't communicate verbally due to brain damage.
The study, published Thursday (Nov. 19) in the journal Science, may help to solve a 150-year-old mystery in neuroscience.

Nowadays, neuroscientists use cutting-edge tools to tease apart the junctions and wiring of our complex brains. But some basic theories in the field are far from new and rest on past discoveries. One of those theories concerns how the brain produces and comprehends speech.

In the 1860s, German neuroanatomist Carl Wernicke identified an area of the brain that is critical to speech and usually found in the temporal lobe on the left side of the organ. Damage to Wernicke's area makes it challenging for people to understand what others are saying — a condition known as Wernicke's aphasia. Therefore, the brain region has been primarily thought of as a decoder that helps us break down the meaning of other people's speech.

But that isn't the whole story. While people who have Wernicke's aphasia can speak in a normal cadence, the words they use don't match their intention. They might substitute semantically related words, with "shoe" becoming "foot," or they might mix up words that have similar sounds, like "leg" and "peg." This can make their sentences sound like nonsensical word salad and thus undermine patients' ability to communicate.

These symptoms make it clear that damage to Wernicke's area affects not just speech comprehension but also speech production. But neuroscientists couldn't identify how this function arose in the brain region or which cells contributed to it.
The question "has remained a mystery for over 150 years now," said study co-author Alexander Silva, a neuroscientist at the University of California, San Francisco.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"One hypothesis is [that] it acts kind of like a proofreader. It listens to you speak, and it corrects errors," Silva explained. "But another is that there's actually dedicated activity in this area that generates upcoming speech."

In their new study, Silva and his colleagues set out to solve the conundrum, using a series of complementary tests that involved recording people's brain activity as they spoke. They had access to powerful tools for understanding brain function, like electrocorticography electrodes, which are implanted onto the brain's surface to measure neural activity. The precision of these tools enabled the team to investigate Wernicke's area at high temporal and spatial resolutions, Silva told Live Science.

The team recruited 28 participants with epilepsy, who already had electrodes implanted to monitor their seizures. They identified a small group of brain cells within Wernicke's area that fired about a quarter of a second before participants spoke words aloud. The signal seemed to be preparing for the speech production, and it could be separated from linked auditory signals made by cells responding to the resulting sound of the spoken words.

But this evidence alone couldn't prove that these cells actually caused speech; it could only correlate the signal with speech production. To connect the dots, the scientists mapped the brains of hundreds of people who were undergoing surgery to have temporal-lobe tumors removed and tested how the surgery affected their speech.

This analysis supported their previous findings; patients were much more likely to have trouble speaking after surgery if the procedure had damaged Wernicke's area, suggesting the area had a role in speech production.

Finally, in 13 people with implanted electrodes and undamaged Wernicke's areas, the researchers tested what happened when they stimulated the brain. When the scientists sent a wave of electricity through the speech-preparation area just before participants opened their mouths to talk, the stimulation caused them to make word errors that resembled Wernicke's aphasia.
The researchers then moved on to a different question: Could these discoveries about Wernicke's area help people whose speech is affected by brain damage?

Using more electrode data, the team identified individual brain cells in Wernicke's area that were linked to saying particular words. Then, they looked at two patients with speech paralysis; these individuals were unable to speak after strokes damaged their brainstems and they'd had electrodes implanted in their brains that sent signals to brain-computer speech devices.

The devices which interpret signals from undamaged areas of the brain to spell out words the patients are trying to say onto a screen. In these patients, the scientists monitored activity from neurons in Wernicke's area with electrodes and were able to decode what the participants were attempting to communicate.
Silva said these discoveries rewrite the textbook on Wernicke's area. Adeen Flinker, a neuroscientist at New York University who was not involved in the study, agreed.
- Ultrasound waves that jiggle deep brain structures may relieve delusions in schizophrenia, small trial hints
- Neuroscience findings often can't be replicated — and it's a big problem for what we know about the brain
- 'It's kind of the holy grail of what is memory': Neuroscientist Steve Ramirez studies the physical basis of memory in a quest to manipulate it
"We already knew that damage to Wernicke's area can lead to speech production errors, but this publication answers why," Flinker told Live Science.

The new findings could lead to better brain-computer interfaces for treating aphasia, Silva said. Until now, patients who have benefited from these interfaces have mainly had problems with the pathways linking their motor cortex and mouth muscles, he said, such as people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

"This is actually a small number of patients relative to the number of patients that have aphasia — so a language disorder from injury to the cortex itself," Silva said. These patients have vocal paralysis but are unable to benefit from BCIs because of this cortical damage, Flinker noted.

This special spot in Wernicke's area could be a new target for brain-computer interfaces aimed at helping patients with aphasia, Silva continued. "We really think that this is an area that could expand the number of people that could benefit from the technology in the near future," he concluded.

He has reported on everything from brain-interface technology to shape-shifting materials science, and from the rise of predatory conferencing to the importance of newborn-screening programs.
